questions.q: Pressing Ctrl+D with a cell selected in Excel will —
options: Copy the content of the cell above into it (fill down)
questions.solution: **Ctrl+D = fill down** — the date stamp is Ctrl+;. Mixing these two is the most repeated Excel trap.

questions.q: The IT Act received its major amendment in —
questions.solution: The **2008 amendment** (effective 2009) added 66C identity theft, 66D cheating, 66F cyber-terrorism and CERT-In's statutory role.

questions.q: Match: 1. Ctrl+D 2. Ctrl+F 3. Ctrl+J — a. find on page b. bookmark c. downloads
questions.solution: Ctrl+**D**rops a bookmark, Ctrl+**F**inds on the page, Ctrl+**J** opens downloads.
questions.shortcut: D bookmark, F find, J downloads.

questions.q: Arrange by **increasing capacity** (single layer): A. DVD  B. CD  C. Blu-ray
questions.solution: CD (700 MB) < DVD (4.7 GB) < Blu-ray (25 GB) — **B, A, C**.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The two leaders held detailed ___ on the border dispute.
questions.solution: 'Held detailed ___ on a dispute' asks for the discussion partnership: **deliberations**. The other options share the -tion shape but belong to wrong topics — parties celebrate, patients take medication, sound reverberates.

questions.q: In the passage, 'no paid leave cushions an illness' suggests that an ill gig worker:
options: has no paid protection to fall back on when sick
must train others during sick leave
receives special leave reserved for illness
gets paid compensation from the platform
questions.solution: The sentence lists what is missing: no minimum wage for waiting hours, no paid leave, pension contributions fully self-funded. *Cushions* here means softens the blow — so a sick gig worker has no paid buffer, **(a)**. (c) and (d) contradict the sentence — paid leave and compensation are exactly what is missing. (b) misreads 'cushion' as a job duty; nothing about training appears.
questions.shortcut: Own-words first: 'cushions an illness' = *protects against the money lost when sick*. Then match.
questions.passage:
The app has changed not only how we order food but what it means to have a job. Across the world, millions now earn through platforms that assign work task by task: a ride, a delivery, a design project. Companies celebrate this flexibility, and for some workers it is real — a student can drive between lectures, a parent can log off when the school day ends. Yet the same arrangement shifts nearly every risk of doing business onto the individual. The platform owns the technology, sets the price and directs the customer to the worker; the worker owns the vehicle, the fuel, the insurance and the idle hours between jobs.

Because a gig worker is classified as an independent partner rather than an employee, she generally falls outside labour laws written for factories and offices. No minimum wage applies to hours spent waiting for a request, no paid leave cushions an illness, and contributions to a pension depend entirely on what the worker chooses, or can afford, to set aside. Several countries are now experimenting with a middle category that would grant platform workers some protections without ending flexible scheduling.

Economists warn that the deeper cost may be invisible: a workforce that cannot plan a month ahead also cannot borrow, train or save with confidence. If algorithms increasingly decide who works and for how much, the question is not whether such work will disappear — it will grow — but whether the rules governing it will grow with it. Societies have rewritten labour law before, when work moved from fields to factories; the same imagination can be applied now.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.  How much ___ does the journey take?
questions.solution: 'Much' goes with an uncountable noun → **time**. 'Hours' is countable and would need 'how many'.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: 'Years later, Arun, now a software engineer, still ___ that pen' — the sentence describes Arun's present habit (note *now*, *still*), with singular subject Arun: **keeps**. *Kept* would clash with 'now/still'; *keep* lacks agreement; *keeping* is not finite.
questions.shortcut: 'Still + now' marks a living present habit → simple present with -s.
questions.passage: When Arun was small, his grandfather took him to the village post office every Saturday. The old man (1) ______ a reply to letters from his brother in Pune, and he insisted that Arun add a line of his own at the bottom. 'A letter carries your handwriting, and handwriting carries your (2) ______,' he would say. Years later, Arun, now a software engineer, still (3) ______ that yellow ink pen in his office drawer, though he rarely posts anything. Last month, when his office announced a drive to send handwritten notes to retired employees, Arun (4) ______ to write fifty of them himself. His colleagues laughed at first; later that day, half of them (5) ______ him at the desk, writing their own notes.

questions.q: **Barren Island**, India's only active volcano, lies in which water body?
questions.solution: **Barren Island** in the **Andaman Sea** (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) erupted again from 1991 onwards; nearby Narcondam is dormant.

questions.q: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was launched in:
questions.solution: **UPI went live in April 2016**, built by NPCI. BHIM, the government's UPI app, followed in December 2016.

questions.q: The Revolt of 1857 **broke out in full** at Meerut on —
questions.solution: On **10 May 1857** the Meerut sepoys mutinied and marched to Delhi, proclaiming Bahadur Shah II. (29 March = Barrackpore/Mangal Pandey.)

questions.q: The **Humayun-nama** was written by —
questions.solution: **Gulbadan Banu Begum**, Humayun's sister, wrote the *Humayun-nama* — a rare woman's inside view of the Mughal household.

questions.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $5$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
questions.solution: CSA $= 2\pi rh = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 5 = 220$ sq cm.
questions.shortcut: $44 \times 5 = 220$. Trap: $154$ — that is a $\pi r^2$ piece (one lid).

questions.q:
Production of a factory (in units):

| Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Units | 480 | 520 | 460 | 540 | 500 | 500 |

If the production of the least productive day is excluded, the average production of the remaining five days (in units) is:
questions.solution: Least day $= 460$. New average $= \frac{3000 - 460}{5} = 508$ units.

questions.q: The solution of $|2x - 1| \ge 5$ is:
questions.solution:
$2x - 1 \ge 5$ gives $x \ge 3$.
$2x - 1 \le -5$ gives $x \le -2$.
Two arms joined by 'or'.

questions.q: It takes $80$ identical tiles to cover a square floor. If the side of the floor is doubled (tiles unchanged), the number of tiles needed is:
questions.solution: Side doubles → area (and tile count) $\times 4$: $80 \times 4 = 320$ tiles.

questions.q:
In the following series, one number is **wrong**. Find the wrong number.

**1, 8, 27, 64, 124, 216**
**|A∩B| = 12, |B∩C| = 10, |A∩C| = 9 and |A∩B∩C| = 5.** How many elements belong to **at least two** of the sets?
questions.solution: At least two = exactly two + all three = (12−5)+(10−5)+(9−5) + 5 = 7+5+4+5 = **21**. Shortcut: pairwise sum 31 counts the triple 3 times → 31 − 2×5 = 21.

questions.q: Select the related number: **6 : 35 :: 9 : ?**
questions.solution: 35 = 36 − 1 = 6² − 1, so the rule is **square then minus 1**. 9² − 1 = **80**. (81 is the plain-square trap.)

questions.solution: A vertical mirror reverses the order and flips every character left-right; top stays top. Read left to right, the image shows **Y E N R U O J**. O, U, Y look the same because they are symmetric about a vertical line; J, R, N, E face the other way. Among the other options, one is flipped characters left in the original order; one is a 180° turn (order reversed and characters upside down); one is the water image (order kept, characters upside down).
questions.shortcut: The image must start with the last character, Y, and nothing may be upside down.
